body.heading: The birthday you did not know you had
paragraphs: In many countries — including Greece, Sweden, Poland, Hungary, Spain, and much of Latin America — people celebrate not only their birthday but their name day: the feast day of the saint, or the calendar day, associated with their first name. For some, the name day is the bigger event, with open-house visiting, flowers, and sweets for colleagues.

The custom has a practical charm: your name day is public knowledge in a way your birthday is not, printed in calendars and announced on the radio in some countries. Nobody has to remember it specially, which means nobody forgets it either.

body.heading: A celebration with the name at the centre
paragraphs: Name days honour the name itself — often chosen for a grandparent, a saint, or a family story — which makes the day a small festival of identity. Children named for someone get a yearly occasion to hear about their namesake.

In Sweden, the calendar printed in almanacs assigns names to nearly every day of the year, and congratulations are expected when yours appears. In Greece, name days can outrank birthdays entirely, especially for adults.

body.heading: Adopt the idea lightly
paragraphs: Even where the custom is not traditional, a family can borrow its spirit: pick the day your calendar assigns, or invent one, and mark each person's name once a year with their favourite meal and the story of why they were given it. Names deserve a day; they are the first gift anyone receives.
The story of a name is worth telling on the day: who chose it, what it means, who else carried it. A child who knows their name's story owns it differently.

description: In Greece, Sweden, Poland, and beyond, the feast day of your first name is a celebration of its own — sometimes bigger than a birthday.
